background.definition: Fecal impaction results when hard, dry stool blocks the intestine, preventing the passage of softer stool. This may completely halt the movement of stool, or may be associated with seepage of liquid stool around the blockage.

list.listitem: The overall prevalence of fecal impaction has not been reported; however, among patients ill enough to undergo surgery, about one-third have palpable fecaliths.
In one study of nursing home patients, about 8% of residents had at least one fecal impaction in a 2-month period.
About 5% to 42% of elderly patients in assisted living facility or hospital settings have fecal impaction
Functional constipation is a common cause in children over 12 months old.
Dietary causes (low fiber diet, dehydration, geophagy).
Drug effects (eg, opiates, anticholinergics, antacids, calcium channel blockers, diuretics, anticholinergics, antipsychotics, calcium and iron supplements).
Metabolic disorders (eg, hypothyroidism, hypokalemia, hypercalcemia).
GI disorders (eg, cystic fibrosis). anal fissure
Intestinal nerve/muscle disorders (eg, Hirschprung's disease).
Neurologic conditions (eg, spina bifida, cerebrovascular accident (CVA)).
Fecal impaction can be both the result and the cause of constipation.
Fecal retention due to reasons listed above, which leads to resorption of salt and water with resultant impaction
A detailed history and physical examination, including digital rectal examination, are often sufficient to diagnose fecal impaction in adults and children. C
In neonates and children, check for red flag causes of symptoms: Hirschprung's disease, spinal deformities and cystic fibrosis other obstruction, fever, elevated white count, bloody diarrhea. C
Consider abdominal imaging: acute abdominal series ( kidney, ureters, bladder - KUB) and CT abdomen in patients with impaction and associated abdominal pain to asess for bowel obstruction

Differential.Differential_Features: No stool in rectum or on abdominal X-ray
No stool in rectum or on abdominal X-ray; other obstruction seen
History of recent abdominal surgery, pancreatitis

list.listitem: Suspect fecal impaction in patients with a history of constipation who complain of abdominal pain, "diarrhea," or encopresis.
Key findings in a child with abdominal pain and constipation include lower left quadrant (LLQ) tenderness without rebound.Stool in the rectal vault is also suggestive of impaction.
In children with encopresis, a history of difficulty with toilet training suggests a diagnosis other than fecal impaction. Absence of stool in the rectal vault makes fecal retention unlikely.

In adults, impaction is often associated with a history of limited mobility, chronic constipation, or use of constipating medications. A nontender abdominal mass may be present. Hard stool is often present in the rectal vault, although its absence does not preclude a more proximal impaction. Diarrhea and fecal incontinence may be present, and compression of the bladder may lead to urinary frequency and urinary incontinence.
Abdominal radiographs are often recommended, especially when history is limited or patient will not consent to digital rectal examination.
However, a recent systematic review suggests that abdominal x-rays in children are of limited usefulness (LR+ 1.0-1.2).
Blood work including CBC, BMP and TSH should be ordered based on the history and clinical exam findings.

While the literature has many case reports of fecaliths mimicking appendicitis, colon cancers and other conditions in children and adults, there are few papers systematically studying radiographs or ultrasounds in adults with fecal impaction.
See algorithm in .
Treatment is aimed at relieving the major complaint and addressing the underlying cause to prevent recurrence. Please see Figure 2
Fecal impaction in the rectum will often require digital fragmentation and mechanical removal. The role of rectal disimpaction in children is unclear
Both oral (PEG, mineral oil) and rectal medications (various enemas, glycerin, mineral oil) are effective for disimpaction. B
Base the choice of treatment on patient and family preferences. C
Few studies of drug therapy for fecal impaction have been placebo controlled; fewer still have directly compared various medications used for disimpaction.
Oral PEG 3350 (brand name Miralax) has been found to be effective for disimpaction in children at doses of 1 to 1.5 g/kg (max. 100 g) daily.
For adults, oral PEG with electrolytes has been effective in small-scale studies in varied populations.
A retrospective cohort found that nasogastric polyethylene glycol was similarly effective with similar adverse effects to oral magnesium citrate.
Oral mineral oil (15-30 mL/y of age, max. 240 mL) is also used for disimpaction for children over 1 year of age.
In infants under 12 months of age, glycerin suppositories have been recommended. Oral mineral oil is not recommended in this age group.
The National Institute for Clinical Excellence recently recommended lubiprostone as a possible treatment for patients with chronic constipation.
While colchicine is more effective than placebo in treating adults with chronic constipation refractory to common treatments, it has not been studied for treating impaction.

A Cochrane review of distal intestinal obstruction syndrome in patients with cystic fibrosis found only a single small crossover trial comparing high and low dose pancreatic enzyme therapy, with no difference reported between groups.
Many agents used for chronic constipation (fiber supplements, colchicine, tegaserod) have not been studied for disimpaction.
Enemas are associated with an increased risk of trauma to the rectal wall.
Phosphate enemas are recommended only after 2 years of age; risk of hyperphosphatemia and hypocalcemia is greatest in patients with renal failure or Hirschprung's disease.
Phosphate enemas are generally not recommended in the elderly because the aforementioned electrolyte derrangements can lead to increased mortality
Magnesium-based enemas are not recommended in infants or children due to potential toxicity (hypermagnesemia, hypophosphatemia, hypocalcemia).
Rectal mineral oil lubricates the stool; although not recommended for infants, it maybe used 1 hour prior to other enemas for children and adults.
For fecal impaction refractory to medications, digital disimpaction and enemas may be treated with endoscopic procedures
Severe cases, though rare, require aggressive manual disimpaction and some sedation in the operating room in order to relax the anal sphincter complex before fecal impaction removal.
Surgical intervention is generally reserved for patients who experience signs and symptoms of peritonitis suggesting colonic perforation.
There are few studies of the well-established practice of manual disimpaction. Guidelines do not address whether or not digital disimpaction should be encouraged in the primary care setting.
Because chronic constipation is associated with a higher rate of colon cancer, colonoscopy may be appropriate after the impaction has been resolved.
In children, effective disimpaction improves symptoms but may not reduce rectal diameter implying that rectal tone may take years to improve. C
A retrospective study revealed that significant mobidity and mortality is associated with fecal impaction in adultsC
Fecal impaction and incontinence are special problems in the nursing home population.
Patients with dementia or limited mobility may not respond to the urge to defecate, leading to constipation and impaction.
A multimodal approach is essential in prevention of chronic constipation in the elderly. See Figure 3.
In neonates, check the patency of the anus.
In neonates and infants with constipation symptoms, consider Hirshsprung's disease.

cell.label: History of constipation. Determine age group.
Meconium absent after 48 hours of life?
Evaluate for possible red flags: fever, vomiting, bloody diarrhea, failure to thrive, analstenosis, tight empty rectum. Red flags present?
Hard mass in lower abdomen without rebound tenderness?
Excessive stool in colon and on abdominal x-ray?
Fecal impaction unlikely; consider other diagnoses and evaluate as appropriate.
Other possible diagnoses (UTI, pneumonia, etc.) eliminated?
Consider colonic perforation or ulceration, with or without impaction.
